title: Teach or bear with them
hook: people exist for one another: teach them, or bear with them (Meditations 8.59)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was aktines, rays that pour out without being used up. Your line was poured out.

Somebody at work does it wrong again. Same report, same mistake, same cheerful shrug. You have a few options. Explain it, one more time. Let it go. Or the third thing, the one that tends to happen without anyone deciding on it: stew, complain about them to someone else, and slowly come to dislike them. Marcus has an entry in book eight only two short sentences long, and it leaves that third option out.
screen: `THE SAME MISTAKE AGAIN.` → `THREE OPTIONS.` → `TEACH OR BEAR WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in George Long's 1862 translation: “Men exist for the sake of one another. Teach them then or bear with them.” That's the whole entry. The reason comes first: people are for each other. The idea comes back again and again in the Meditations. We're made to work together, like hands, or feet, or eyelids, or the rows of upper and lower teeth, an image he used back in book two. If that's true, the person who frustrates you is still someone you exist for. Then two doors. If you can show them a better way, teach. Not lecture, not win: teach, which means you actually want them to understand. And if you can't, because they won't listen, or it isn't your place, or you've already tried, then bear with them. Put up with them. Carry it. Now notice what isn't on the list: resent them, gossip about them, write them off. Marcus doesn't argue against those here. He just doesn't offer them, and so the note quietly shuts that third door. It works in both directions, too. Somewhere, someone is deciding right now whether to teach you or bear with you.
screen: `MEN EXIST FOR ONE ANOTHER.` · `MADE TO WORK TOGETHER.` · `DOOR ONE: TEACH. DOOR TWO: BEAR.` · `NO THIRD DOOR.` · then, large: `TEACH OR BEAR.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who frustrates you in a small, ordinary way, and ask honestly: is there a kind, clear way to show them, one they could actually hear? If yes, picture saying it gently, once. If no, picture bearing it, letting it pass through you without the stewing, and breathe with the door you chose.
Third door. The one option Marcus leaves off his list when he says teach them or bear with them: resent, gossip, write them off. Today's word.
Your line: teach or bear. Two doors, both kind, and no third. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: People who live by this line of Marcus often make the choice consciously when someone frustrates them: either explain once, kindly, or let it go without resentment.
